summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Quindío is the national Colombian one, and it is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The source inventory contains no Quindío-specific legal, enforcement or incident finding. Nothing in it deviates from the national position far enough to be scored separately, so the department is assessed at the national score, and the findings below are national context that a visitor to Quindío should expect to carry across departmental lines.

The gap between the statutory framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025. The Guardian reports 41 trans people killed in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Lethal anti-trans violence is not confined to remote territory. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in broad daylight on 4 April 2025 in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín; the assault was filmed and the 28-second video went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she died of cardiac arrest that afternoon. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". Police questioned local residents and President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, but no one was arrested, and solidarity events were held in several cities.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate, including in territories under their control. In Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyers on the street and via WhatsApp, naming "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots" and "faggots, lesbians and men and women who destroy homes" as legitimate military targets, and threatened a further wave. Three armed men gave a trans woman and local election candidate one week to leave town; she hid for a week, then fled at night. A second trans woman said a friend of hers was killed, and Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Trans women in these departments reported few options beyond hairdressing or sex work, with discrimination narrowing their livelihoods to those two trades.

The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity.
tangentialFactors:
The national counts move in both directions across the sources, which is worth holding together rather than reading as a single trend: 41 trans people killed in 2023, eight between February and April 2024, 13 in the first quarter of 2025, and 35 LGBTI murders of all kinds between January and May 2025 as recorded by the Attorney General's Office. The figures come from different counting bodies and different definitions of victim category, so they are not directly comparable.

Two distinct violence regimes coexist in the country. One is territorial, driven by armed groups issuing flyer and WhatsApp kill lists and forcing named trans women out of towns, as documented in Caquetá and Guajira. The other is ordinary urban homicide in daylight, filmed and circulated, as in Bello, Antioquia, where a presidential order for an urgent investigation still produced no arrest. A visitor to Quindío faces the second regime by default and the first only where armed actors are present.

The economic squeeze on trans women is reported as a driver of exposure: discrimination limits them mainly to hairdressing or sex work, and in Caquetá trans women reported few options beyond sex work. Confinement to street-facing or client-facing work raises the number of encounters in which hostility can occur.

Displacement as a tactic is documented alongside killing. A trans election candidate in Caquetá was given a week to leave and fled at night; a trans salon owner relocated twice after death threats. Threats that end in relocation rather than death still end in the loss of a home and a business.

International scrutiny is active and recent. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the pattern of violence, and the UN Independent Expert Graeme Reid's May 2025 mission praised the reforms while stating that institutional progress and lived experience are disconnected.

Whether armed-group "social cleansing" campaigns, flyer kill lists or forced displacement have reached Quindío is not sourced. The documented campaigns are in Caquetá and Guajira, and their territorial extent beyond those departments is unresolved.
